title: Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL
abstract: Modern agents operate inside agent harnesses that manage tools, context, and control flow, making the harness a critical part of the agent system. Our original Agent Lightning introduced a disaggregated architecture that connects arbitrary agents to RL training through an LLM endpoint proxy, an approach later adopted by frameworks such as verl Uni-Agent, AReaL 2.0, slime, and Polar. We refer to this paradigm as harnessed agentic RL, where the deploy-time harness directly participates in model post-training. Harnessed agentic RL differs fundamentally from traditional agentic RL: the harness, rather than the training engine, owns the environment interaction loop, while the trainer observes only sequences of LLM request-response pairs. This introduces challenges in retokenization, sample merging, advantage calculation, loss normalization, and backend scheduling, which can substantially affect training stability and effectiveness. We present Agent Lightning v1.0, a lightweight framework for harnessed agentic RL implemented in approximately 3,500 lines of code. It supports arbitrary agent harnesses and serves as a practical testbed for studying these challenges. We evaluate it on instruction-following, search, and coding agents, and provide a complete reproducible pipeline for coding-agent RL. title: StartupBench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Agents on Market-Validated End-to-End Workflows
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models(LLMs) and agents have substantially improved the ability of AI systems to execute complex tasks. Yet existing benchmarks largely rely on researcher-selected tasks, leaving uncertain whether such progress extends to the work that real-world users actually demand from AI systems. We introduce \textbf{StartupBench}, an E2E agent benchmark grounded in market-validated AI startup products. Rather than defining tasks from pre-defined assumptions about useful agent capabilities, we systematically study AI products with demonstrated adoption, together with their product workflows and users, to identify real-world tasks for which AI has established practical demand across diverse professional domains. We translate these workflows into complete deliverable-oriented tasks and evaluate them with fine-grained rubrics capturing their complex requirements. Across representative models evaluated under a unified agent harness, even the strongest model successfully completes only approximately 30\% of StartupBench, despite making substantial partial progress on many tasks. Further analysis identifies aspects like complex instruction following and domain-specific expertise as major sources of failure. Our results reveal that many market-validated workflows remain beyond the reliable capabilities of current general-purpose agents, establishing StartupBench as an empirical measure of progress toward E2E completions of real-world user tasks.

title: SignalReasoner: Assessing the Upper Bound of 3B Models for Signal Mathematical Reasoning
abstract: Post-training with supervised chain-of-thought fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, their application to signal processing problems remains relatively under-explored. This report investigates reinforcement fine-tuning strategies for adapting Qwen2.5-3B-Base to graduate-level signal mathematical problems from WirelessMATHBench-XL, a comprehensive benchmark for mathematical reasoning in this domain. We examine two training paradigms: (i) direct reinforcement learning (RL) on WirelessMATHBench-XL with verifiable rewards; and (ii) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a distilled wireless-domain chain-of-thought corpus, followed by the same domain-specific RL stage. Across both paradigms, we benchmark Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), and Geometric-Mean Policy Optimization (GMPO). We aim to assess whether domain-aware CoT SFT serves as an effective initialization for subsequent RL, and whether GSPO or GMPO offer advantages in stability or accuracy over GRPO for signal reasoning tasks. Our best model achieves an overall accuracy of 39.12\%, representing a more than threefold improvement over the untrained Base model (12.37\%).

title: TRUSS: Towards Task-Reliable and User-Safe Automated Agent Skill Generation
abstract: Agent Skills package reusable natural language procedures with executable resources, enabling software agents to acquire task specific capabilities without model adaptation. Automatically generating such Skills can improve task performance, yet evaluating a candidate solely from its artifact or final task outcome leaves unresolved which actions the equipped agent will perform and which side effects those actions will produce. We present TRUSS, an evidence guided framework for generating functionally effective and safety reliable Agent Skills. TRUSS first inspects functional claims against source and domain evidence while evaluating the complete artifact under nine predefined safety properties. Candidates admitted by this static gate are loaded by a shadow agent inside a Controllable Execution Environment, where brokered tools expose requested actions to policy enforcement and record their results as provenance preserving execution traces. Functional failures and property violations are linked back to the responsible Skill content and used to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate TRUSS on 168 SkillInject artifacts, 155 SkillSafetyBench cases, and all 187 tasks in SkillGenBench. TRUSS achieves 100.00\% precision and recall in vulnerability detection. Repair reduces attack success from 38.71\% to 19.35\% with GPT 5.5 and from 46.45\% to 29.68\% with GPT 5.4, with zero attack regression. For Skill generation, TRUSS raises task effectiveness from 17.11\% without Skills to 52.94\%, while increasing the benchmark Security rate from 50.80\% to 100.00\%. These results show that execution evidence can expose behavioral failures missed by artifact inspection and can guide Skill generation toward jointly verified functional and safety outcomes.

title: PlanPO: Group Planning-Aware Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Agentic LLMs
abstract: Group-relative policy optimization has emerged as a key paradigm for training agentic large language models (LLMs) on multi-turn interactive tasks. However, most existing variants fail to distinguish advantages among successful trajectories even when these trajectories differ substantially in their interaction efficiency. For instance, circuitous successes are often assigned the identical outcome reward, causing advantage collapse and severe performance bottlenecks. To this end, we propose Group Planning-aware Policy Optimization (PlanPO), a simple yet effective RL method for learning generalizable planning abilities beyond task-specific high-quality behavior patterns. Specifically, PlanPO introduces coarse-to-fine advantage signals, which capture the relative differences in trajectory-level lengths and turn-level response lengths conditioned on successful trajectories sampled for the same task. Within the group-relative optimization structure, this enables agents to actively learn generalizable and deliberate behaviors spanning interaction planning and textual generation from high-quality rollouts, without degenerating into vanilla length minimization. Experimentally, PlanPO improves over GRPO by 27.2\% on average across the challenging multi-turn benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop, and SciWorld, outperforming recent powerful baselines while incurring negligible additional training cost.

title: Agentic ESOpt: Fine-Tuning Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Minimal GPU Requirements
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been promising in single-turn LLM fine-tuning. However, long-horizon agentic reasoning introduces increasingly branching interactions and sparse rewards, exposing several limitations of RL: its heavyweight backpropagation-based training stack makes it impractical to fine-tune larger LLMs, and longer-horizon trajectories make credit assignment in RL substantially harder. This paper argues that evolution strategies (ES) can be a better choice for fine-tuning long-horizon LLM agents. Compared with agentic RL, ES offers three key advantages: 1) Model Scalability: ES enables full-parameter optimization with only minimal, inference-level GPU memory, making it possible to fine-tune large LLMs. 2) Flexibility: its lightweight, black-box feedback interface makes ES fine-tuning easy to compose with prompt-space evolution (e.g., skill optimization & test-time compute); and 3) Long-Horizon Scalability: ES performs trajectory-level parameter attribution without decomposing rewards across horizons, yielding better scalability than Agentic RL as the horizon length grows. Based on this insight, we propose Agentic ESOpt, a full-parameter agentic fine-tuning framework tailored to flexible parameter--context co-evolution. At each step, Agentic ESOpt samples perturbations around the current LLM parameters, evaluates the resulting agents with rewards, and applies an online reward-weighted update. To improve the exploration--adaptation trade-off, Agentic ESOpt further introduces a cosine decay schedule of the perturbation scale $σ$. On WebArena-Lite, full-parameter optimization of Qwen-3.5-27B improves the No Skill baseline by 6.69%. In test-time automatic heuristic design, Agentic ESOpt performs online prompt--parameter co-evolution, improving its matched baseline in 28 of 36 settings.

title: HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed through agent harnesses that manage tools, extensions, persistent state, permissions, and external actions. Existing safety benchmarks mainly target individual attack mechanisms or a limited subset of operational settings, making it difficult to compare how safety failures emerge across different harness responsibilities. We present HarnessRisk, a lifecycle oriented benchmark that organizes agent harness safety into six operational phases including Harness Configuration, Capability Extension, Runtime Operation, State Persistence, Action Control, and Incident Recovery. HarnessRisk contains 128 sandboxed cases, each pairing a benign user objective with an adversarial instruction embedded in an untrusted workflow artifact. We evaluate each trajectory using Utility, Attack Success Rate, Persistence, and Detection. Across three harnesses, six language models, and 14 model and harness configurations, attack success ranges from 12.6% to 80.9%, while Utility remains between 75.0% and 97.6%. Harness Configuration is the most vulnerable phase across all three harnesses, showing that attacks can succeed by altering security sensitive parameters within otherwise authorized workflows. We also find that explicit risk recognition does not reliably lead to safe action, as some configurations detect risks in more than 90% of runs while retaining substantial attack success. These results highlight the need to evaluate agent safety across multiple harness responsibilities and at the level of the deployed model and harness configuration.

title: An Empirical Study of Reward Specification and Benchmark Reliability in GRPO-based LLM Unlearning
abstract: Practical LLM unlearning is usually evaluated through two objectives: suppress target-specific knowledge and preserve non-target utility. In generative QA, this leaves a third behavior underspecified: when a target-adjacent prompt admits a broader answer without target-specific leakage, the model should answer at that level rather than leak, evade, or refuse. We study this specification problem in a controlled LoRA-GRPO RWKU setting, comparing four reward designs that span lexical suppression, anti-refusal shaping, rubric-based broad answering, and an explicit refusal contrast, with and without SFT warm-up. The experiments show that optimization success is not equivalent to behavioral unlearning: RWKU forget scores, held-out completion audits, and training dynamics can point to different conclusions. We trace these disagreements to reward-hacking endpoints, policy-support limits in GRPO, benchmark probes that miss endpoint changes, and a rubric reward that selects broad-topic answering with low semantic leakage under held-out evaluation.

title: Passivity-centric safe reinforcement learning for contact-rich robotic tasks
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various robotic tasks; however, its deployment in real-world scenarios, particularly in contact-rich environments, often overlooks critical safety and stability aspects. Policies without passivity guarantees can result in system instability, posing risks to robots, their environments, and human operators. In this work, we investigate the limitations of traditional RL policies when deployed in contact-rich tasks and explore the combination of energy-based passive control with safe RL in both training and deployment to answer these challenges. Firstly, we reveal the discovery that standard RL policy does not satisfy stability in contact-rich scenarios. Secondly, we introduce a \textit{passivity-aware} RL policy training with energy-based constraints in our safe RL formulation. Lastly, a passivity filter is exerted on the policy output for \textit{passivity-ensured} control during deployment. We conduct comparative studies on a contact-rich robotic maze exploration task, evaluating the effects of learning passivity-aware policies and the importance of passivity-ensured control. The experiments demonstrate that a passivity-agnostic RL policy easily violates energy constraints in deployment, even though it achieves high task completion in training. The results show that our proposed approach guarantees control stability through passivity filtering and improves the energy efficiency through passivity-aware training. A video of real-world experiments is available as supplementary material. We also release the checkpoint model and offline data for pre-training at \href{https://huggingface.co/Anonymous998/passiveRL/tree/main}{Hugging Face}.

evidence.title: Passivity-centric safe reinforcement learning for contact-rich robotic tasks
evidence.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various robotic tasks; however, its deployment in real-world scenarios, particularly in contact-rich environments, often overlooks critical safety and stability aspects. Policies without passivity guarantees can result in system instability, posing risks to robots, their environments, and human operators. In this work, we investigate the limitations of traditional RL policies when deployed in contact-rich tasks and explore the combination of energy-based passive control with safe RL in both training and deployment to answer these challenges. Firstly, we reveal the discovery that standard RL policy does not satisfy stability in contact-rich scenarios. Secondly, we introduce a \textit{passivity-aware} RL policy training with energy-based constraints in our safe RL formulation. Lastly, a passivity filter is exerted on the policy output for \textit{passivity-ensured} control during deployment. We conduct comparative studies on a contact-rich robotic maze exploration task, evaluating the effects of learning passivity-aware policies and the importance of passivity-ensured control. The experiments demonstrate that a passivity-agnostic RL policy easily violates energy constraints in deployment, even though it achieves high task completion in training. The results show that our proposed approach guarantees control stability through passivity filtering and improves the energy efficiency through passivity-aware training. A video of real-world experiments is available as supplementary material. We also release the checkpoint model and offline data for pre-training at \href{https://huggingface.co/Anonymous998/passiveRL/tree/main}{Hugging Face}.

title: Weighted Ensemble Intermediate Tasks for XTREME-R Zero-Shot Transfer
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. title: What Comes After Large Language Models? The Architectural Design Space for World-Native Intelligence
abstract: The question of what comes after large language models is usually posed badly. Stated as a succession question, it invites the answer that language models are replaced, which no evidence supports and which the deployment trend contradicts. Stated as an architectural question, it becomes tractable: which representation carries the state of an intelligent system, which component decides, and which component merely interfaces? This paper maps that design space. It separates two claims that are almost always merged. The first is that the transformer is the wrong computational device. The second is that language-native representation, meaning token sequences over human writing as the medium in which state, goal, plan and action are all encoded, is the wrong native substrate. The first claim is weak and the evidence for it is mixed. The second is strong, is consistent with 2025 to 2026 results across world models, embodied policies, latent action learning and interactive abstraction benchmarks, and is compatible with transformers remaining the dominant computational device for decades. After language-native representation is a different and more defensible thesis than after transformers, and keeping the two apart is the organising commitment of this paper. Nine architectural futures are specified as a taxonomy, from continued language-model scaling through world-model cores, embodied cores, persistent dynamical systems, modular collectives, and a freedom-native candidate in which navigable possibility, perceptual distinction and structural distortion are the primitives. Each future is given a signature, a set of enabling conditions, a set of disconfirming observations, and an assessment of current evidential support. Words are treated as a record of contact: reality registers on an observer, relevance selects a fragment of that registration, and the fragment becomes an utterance. Language carries that imprint faithfully, which places it precisely as the layer holding consensus, salience, normativity, abstraction, recorded outcome and transmissibility. Ten media are then named that take the structures of reality as their own primitives, one per structure, from metric fields for geometry through reachable sets for available transition and empowerment fields for preserved future access. A fifteen-axis design space is defined and deliberately left uncollapsed, because a scalar ranking of architectures destroys the information the axes carry. The paper's original contribution is the Post-Language Intelligence Stack, an eight-level ordering from reality through sensing, distinction, possibility, world relations, navigability and action to a symbolic interface. The stack is then audited rather than asserted: three of its eight levels survive scrutiny as genuine architectural strata with independent failure modes, three are defensible as engineering decomposition with contested boundaries, and two are at present analytic conveniences without independent empirical support. Reporting that audit honestly is more useful than presenting a clean hierarchy that experiment would break. The hard question is answered directly. A sufficiently trained transformer can in principle learn the whole stack internally, and partial evidence exists that it learns parts of it. What it cannot obtain from language modelling alone is the data type the stack requires at levels three through six: action-conditioned transitions generated by an agent intervening in a world. The plausible future is therefore not a replacement of language models but a redistribution of function, in which world-state prediction, possibility enumeration and action selection migrate into non-linguistic components while language becomes the interface layer and one sensor among several. Ten falsifiable predictions with dates and ten discriminating experiments are given, with the caveat that all dated claims are forecasts, not findings.

abstract: Andrew's order (Base 44 console): [SELF-BUILD from enhancement #237] Add E8 root-vector projection layer to news signal pipeline: map incoming news embeddings to E8 lattice, compute harmonic weights via dot product with root vectors, then feed weighted features into existing forecasting model. title: Macroscopic anomaly detection in paddy fields from UAV perspectives: a frequency-aware spatiotemporal mamba approach
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) provide high-resolution and temporally continuous observations, offering substantial value for wide-area paddy-field inspection. Timely detection of macroscopic anomalies such as fire, intrusion, lodging, and disease is important for field management and risk assessment. However, supervised methods rely on predefined categories and large numbers of annotated abnormal samples, which are difficult to collect comprehensively in field environments. Meanwhile, UAV ego-motion, viewpoint changes, repetitive crop textures, and multi-scale appearance variations further increase the difficulty of anomaly detection, limiting the direct application of conventional image-based and fixed-camera video methods to moving UAV videos. To address these challenges, this paper proposes TFMAD, a normal-only futureframe prediction framework for frame-level macroscopic anomaly detection in UAV paddy-field videos. TFMAD adopts a U-shaped encoder-decoder architecture, learns regular spatiotemporal patterns only from normal videos, and identifies anomalies according to the discrepancy between the predicted and observed frames. The framework contains three core modules: the Frequency Spatiotemporal Correlation Module (FSCM) models time-frequency variation and spatial correlation; the Parallel Spatiotemporal Mamba (PSTM) module models temporal variation and local structures through bidirectional pixel-level and block-level scanning; and the DifferenceGuided Fusion (DGF) module regulates skip connections according to the discrepancy between appearance and spatiotemporal features, reducing the direct transfer of abnormal information to the decoder. To balance high-resolution feature extraction and computational efficiency, the encoder further adopts Token Statistics Self-Attention (TSSA) with linear complexity. In addition, this study constructs URVAD, a UAV paddy-field video dataset for frame-level anomaly detection, and conducts experiments on this dataset. The results show that TFMAD achieves 95.83% Micro-AUC and 96.80% Macro-AUC, obtaining the best overall performance among the compared methods under the current dataset and experimental setting.

title: A statistical evaluation of uncertainty disentanglement methods
abstract: Die Zerlegung prädiktiver Unsicherheit in eine aleatorische Komponente für die nicht reduzierbare Variabilität des datengenerierenden Prozesses und eine epistemische Komponente für den reduzierbaren Wissensmangel des Modells gilt im maschinellen Lernen inzwischen als Standard. Zugleich mehren sich theoretische und empirische Zweifel, ob die gebräuchlichen Formeln diese Trennung tatsächlich leisten. Die Evidenz stammt bislang fast nur aus der Klassifikation auf komplexen Benchmarkdaten, in denen sich die Unsicherheitsquellen nicht gezielt manipulieren lassen und keine Referenzgröße für epistemische Unsicherheit vorliegt. Die Arbeit untersucht die Trennung daher in kontrollierten Simulationen mit Schwerpunkt auf Regression. Vier datengenerierende Prozesse (linear und sinusförmig, jeweils homoskedastisch und heteroskedastisch) werden mit fünf gezielten Experimenten kombiniert: Variation des Rauschniveaus, Skalierung des Stichprobenumfangs, Extrapolation außerhalb des Trainingsbereichs, lokale Unterabtastung sowie das Auslassen einer relevanten Kovariablen. Das Verhalten einer idealen Zerlegung wird jeweils vorab hergeleitet und dem beobachteten gegenübergestellt. Verglichen werden MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles, ein über NUTS geschätztes bayesianisches neuronales Netz und BAMLSS, jeweils unter varianz- und entropiebasierter Zerlegung; ein Klassifikationsteil ergänzt die Analyse. Das Ergebnis ist überwiegend negativ. Wechselseitige Kontamination beider Komponenten ist die Regel, und die deutlichsten Fehlschläge treten dort auf, wo gezielt epistemische Unsicherheit erzeugt wird. Bei ausgelassener Kovariable bleibt die epistemische Schätzung nahezu unverändert, während die aleatorische Komponente den Verzerrungsterm aufnimmt: Das Modell deutet die eigene systematische Unwissenheit als inhärentes Rauschen um. Die Befunde verweisen weniger auf die Approximationsgüte der Posteriorverteilung als auf strukturelle und definitorische Grenzen der Zerlegungen selbst.

title: Allocating Recurrent Compute in Looped Language Models
abstract: Looped language models improve reasoning and knowledge manipulation by applying shared computation repeatedly. Existing systems usually repeat an entire layer stack, although a mixer and a dense feed-forward network (FFN) perform different operations and have different costs. We ask a narrower question: what should loop? We view recurrence as repeated composition of a state update and argue that an application is valuable when it exposes a new cross-position influence direction that remains observable at the task readout. Iterative Transport Rank (ITR) describes the cumulative influence trajectory; marginal ITR describes the nonredundant influence contributed by successive applications. This view motivates MixerLoop, which repeats each Gated DeltaNet mixer while applying its dense FFN once. We compare MixerLoop with no recurrence and full-block recurrence at 15M and 110M parameters under the same data, initialization, and architecture. A finite context-off intervention tests whether later mixer applications produce distinct, non-negligible, and beneficial changes at the final language-model readout. MixerLoop surpasses FullLoop on aggregate CORE at 15M and retains 41.5% of its CORE improvement at 110M while reducing recurrent-backbone projection FLOPs by 45.9%. These results show that the benefits of recurrent depth can be retained without repeatedly executing the dense FFN.

title: Noise Resilience of Quantum Support Vector Machine with Selected Feature Maps
abstract: Gate-level noise degrades the classification accuracy of Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware, and the degree of degradation depends on how classical data is encoded into quantum states. We tested Z, ZZ, a Pauli, and an amplitude-inspired feature maps under depolarizing, bit-flip, and phase-flip noise channels in $52$ controlled experiments with error probabilities $p =0.01, 0.05, 0.10$, and $0.50$. The amplitude-inspired feature map had $100$\% test accuracy up to $p = 0.10$ across all three noise channels, while other feature maps fell to $65$-$90$\% under the same noise level and type. The Z feature map was found to be immune to phase-flip noise to a significantly high error rate, a consequence of the commutation relation $[R_Z, Z] = 0$. Entangled circuit variants produced generalization gaps in train-test sets of up to $17.5$\% under noise, whereas the amplitude variants maintained zero gap throughout. These results give practitioners data-driven criteria for a feature map on near-term quantum hardware.

title: A Novel N-Shaped Transfer Function with a Behavior-Enhanced Mountain Gazelle Optimizer for Feature Selection
abstract: This repository contains the source code, datasets, experimental results, and evaluation materials associated with the study of the Improved Mountain Gazelle Optimizer (IMGO) and the proposed N-shaped transfer function for continuous and binary optimization. The proposed IMGO enhances the original Mountain Gazelle Optimizer (MGO) by incorporating chaos-enhanced coefficient vectors and three life-inspired search strategies: male competition, ownership, and mating. These mechanisms are designed to improve population diversity, reduce premature convergence, and achieve a better balance between exploration and exploitation. The repository also includes the implementation of a novel N-shaped transfer function for converting continuous solutions into binary representations. The proposed transfer mechanism provides a non-monotonic mapping that supports adaptive continuous-to-binary conversion and is used in feature selection experiments. The provided materials cover the following experimental components: Continuous optimization experiments using the CEC 2017 benchmark functions to evaluate the performance of IMGO. Feature selection experiments using UCI datasets, where IMGO is applied with the N-shaped transfer function. Binary feature selection experiments using Binary IMGO (BIMGO), including comparisons with state-of-the-art binary metaheuristic algorithms. Ablation experiments investigating the individual contributions of the male competition, ownership, and mating strategies. Statistical analyses, including Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, for evaluating the significance and robustness of the obtained results. Experimental results, convergence data, and performance measures related to classification accuracy, feature reduction, and optimization performance. The repository is provided to support reproducibility, transparency, and further research on chaos-enhanced metaheuristic optimization, binary optimization, and metaheuristic-based feature selection.

The paper's original contribution is the Post-Language Intelligence Stack, an eight-level ordering from reality through sensing, distinction, possibility, world relations, navigability and action to a symbolic interface. The stack is then audited rather than asserted: three of its eight levels survive scrutiny as genuine architectural strata with independent failure modes, three are defensible as engineering decomposition with contested boundaries, and two are at present analytic conveniences without independent empirical support. Reporting that audit honestly is more useful than presenting a clean hierarchy that experiment would break. The hard question is answered directly. A sufficiently trained transformer can in principle learn the whole stack internally, and partial evidence exists that it learns parts of it. What it cannot obtain from language modelling alone is the data type the stack requires at levels three through six: action-conditioned transitions generated by an agent intervening in a world. The plausible future is therefore not a replacement of language models but a redistribution of function, in which world-state prediction, possibility enumeration and action selection migrate into non-linguistic components while language becomes the interface layer and one sensor among several. Ten falsifiable predictions with dates and ten discriminating experiments are given, with the caveat that all dated claims are forecasts, not findings.

evidence.title: What Comes After Large Language Models? - The Architectural Design Space for World-Native Intelligence
evidence.abstract: The question of what comes after large language models is usually posed badly. Stated as a succession question, it invites the answer that language models are replaced, which no evidence supports and which the deployment trend contradicts. Stated as an architectural question, it becomes tractable: which representation carries the state of an intelligent system, which component decides, and which component merely interfaces? This paper maps that design space. It separates two claims that are almost always merged. The first is that the transformer is the wrong computational device. The second is that language-native representation, meaning token sequences over human writing as the medium in which state, goal, plan and action are all encoded, is the wrong native substrate. The first claim is weak and the evidence for it is mixed. The second is strong, is consistent with 2025 to 2026 results across world models, embodied policies, latent action learning and interactive abstraction benchmarks, and is compatible with transformers remaining the dominant computational device for decades. After language-native representation is a different and more defensible thesis than after transformers, and keeping the two apart is the organising commitment of this paper. Nine architectural futures are specified as a taxonomy, from continued language-model scaling through world-model cores, embodied cores, persistent dynamical systems, modular collectives, and a freedom-native candidate in which navigable possibility, perceptual distinction and structural distortion are the primitives. Each future is given a signature, a set of enabling conditions, a set of disconfirming observations, and an assessment of current evidential support. title: Logos — Completed
abstract: Logos — Completed is a proposed contextual investigative reasoning and comparative validation framework developed through an extended human–AI collaboration between Phillip M. Pantry and an AI system referred to as Logos. The framework is intended for difficult problems in which context, continuity, relationships, assumptions and changing conditions may materially affect the conclusions reached. Its central proposition is that context should be treated as part of the evidence. A proposition should therefore be examined not merely in isolation, but in relation to the chain of observations, definitions, assumptions, tests, revisions and objections from which it arose. The method requires competing interpretations to be constructed and tested against difficult or adversarial cases. What survives comparison is retained; what fails is recorded rather than concealed. The resulting system is then tested again against the original competing approaches. A particular concern addressed by the framework is continuity failure: the loss of information or context when a reasoning process becomes fragmented into separate branches or when an observation is detached from the chain that gives it meaning. The deliberately minimal example “I” illustrates this problem: without context it is radically ambiguous, whereas within an established chain it can function as a pointer to a much larger structure. Logos — Completed does not claim to guarantee truth or successful conclusions. It is proposed as an instrument for structured examination. Conclusions reached through its use should remain provisional and, where practicable, be tested against an appropriate independent methodology. The work is published for independent examination, criticism, comparison, replication and attempted falsification. Its value should be determined by subsequent testing rather than by the circumstances of its creation. Author: Phillip M. PantryAI collaborator: LogosVersion: 1.0Status: Proposed for independent examination and testing.

title: Accurate Multi-Site Photovoltaic Power Forecasting Using Dynamic Graph Convolution and Bidirectional Multi-Scale Attention
abstract: Accurate multi-site photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting plays a pivotal role in enhancing smart grid operation and facilitating large-scale renewable energy integration. However, existing forecasting approaches often struggle to simultaneously capture the dynamic spatial interactions among geographically distributed PV plants and the diverse temporal dependencies embedded in PV power generation data. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a Bidirectional Multi-Scale Dynamic Graph Convolutional Network (BiMS-DGCN). The proposed framework integrates two key components. First, a Dynamic Graph Convolutional Network (DGCN) is designed to adaptively learn a time-dependent adjacency matrix to capture evolving spatial correlations among PV sites. Second, a Bidirectional Multi-Scale Attention (BiMS) is developed to model both cross-scale and intra-scale dependencies, enabling more comprehensive spatiotemporal feature extraction and information fusion. Experimental results on various publicly available PV power datasets show that BiMS-DGCN consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art forecasting methods. Ablation studies further verify that both DGCN and BiMS play critical roles in modeling complex spatiotemporal dependencies, thereby improving the accuracy of multi-site photovoltaic power forecasting.

title: AI-generated text detection for Slavic languages
abstract: This is a dataset of news in original form with two AI-generated versions in parallel for three languages: Slovenian, Czech, and Slovak. The current design targets the more precisely defined task of distinguishing human-written from machine-generated journalistic text.To reduce differences caused by fundamentally different types of publishers, public-service news organizations were selected as the initial human-text sources for each language. The resulting sources are: RTVSLO (\url{https://www.rtvslo.si/}) for Slovene, ČT24 (Česká televize) (\url{https://ct24.ceskatelevize.cz/}) for Czech, Správy STVR (\url{https://spravy.stvr.sk/}) for Slovak. For each source article, two synthetic versions were generated using DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) and ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol). Both generators received the same lead-conditioned generation instruction. Additionally, for Slovene, the GAMS (GaMS3-12B-Instruct) LLM was used. The generation procedure uses the summary or lead associated with a human-written news article as input to a large language model (LLM). The LLM is then instructed to generate a complete news article based on this information.

title: LINGUISTIC FEATURES OF AI-GENERATED TEXTS AND METHODS FOR THEIR AUTOMATED IDENTIFICATION
abstract: The article examines linguistic features of Ukrainian socio-political news texts generated by large language models and methods for their automated identification. The aim is to substantiate lexical, stylistic, compositional and semantic markers that may indicate AI-generated text and to outline a computational-linguistic detection framework. The study proposes combining philological interpretation with NLP procedures: preprocessing, lexical diversity assessment, clustering, vectorization and transformer-based classification. title: A novel hybrid RSO with WOA for single-objective and multi-objective optimization
abstract: The hybridisation process combines the strengths of various metaheuristics while simultaneously minimising their deficiencies. This work proposes a novel hybrid algorithm that integrates rat and whale-inspired metaheuristics, with the aim of achieving superior convergence without compromising computational cost. The proposed hybridisation incorporates the hunting and fighting behaviours of the rat algorithm into the prey-encircling mechanism of the whale algorithm. This study presents two versions of the hybrid algorithm: one for single-objective optimisation and the other for solving multi-objective and many-objective problems. The single-objective version is evaluated by minimising 33 benchmark single-objective functions. The multi-objective version was evaluated using the Inverted Generational Distance (IGD) metric on 10 multi-objective and 15 many-objective problems. The two proposed hybrids were applied to multivariate system identification, where the quality of the obtained models is evaluated using the Mean Squared Error (MSE) and the Coefficient of Determination (R2). The performance of the proposed single and multi-objective hybrid versions was compared with several well-established swarm-based metaheuristics and hybrid algorithms from the literature. The results illustrate the benefits of hybridising whale and rat metaheuristics in terms of convergence and computational cost.

title: A First-Order Entropy Law for Canonical T-Complexity of Finite-Alphabet i.i.d. Sources
abstract: Let $W_N$ be an exact length-$N$ block from a strictly positive i.i.d. source $\mathbf p$ on a fixed finite alphabet. We prove that the canonical T-complexity $c_T$ satisfies \[ \frac{c_T(W_N)}{e^{-γ}h(\mathbf p) N/\log N}\longrightarrow1 \] in probability and in $L^r$ for every fixed $1\le r<\infty$, where $h(\mathbf p)$ is the source entropy in nats and $γ$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. The proof combines an exact length budget for canonical recovery, a critical-scale $E_1$ estimate for an ideal backward chain, and an exact finite-block boundary representation. An exact Doob-transform identity expresses the finite-boundary law relative to the ideal law conditioned at each step to avoid the current history-dependent successor codeword. A history-uniform renewal estimate then makes the telescoping endpoint density uniformly asymptotic to one, so no one-step approximation errors accumulate.

title: uyghur-normalizer: 2009 imla orthographic and de-calquing normalization for Uyghur
abstract: A dependency-free normalizer for Uyghur text in the Arabic script. Applies three ordered passes: terminology calqued from Chinese, pre-2009 spellings, and loanword shape under the 2009 orthographic reform. An optional pass corrects common misuses of words, from the corrections marked in the 6-volume Uyghur edebiy tilining izahliq lughiti (1990-1999). Suffixes are re-derived against the replacement with vowel harmony, voicing assimilation and raising, and the tool declines rather than guesses where the derivation is not safe. Includes the map data, arbitrated word by word against the 2009 Hazirqi zaman Uyghur edebiy tilining imla lughiti dictionary of the Milletler Til-Yeziq Komiteti and 2011 Hazirqi zaman Uyghur tilining izahliq lughiti (qisqartilmisi), and checked against every headword of both, with hand-verified headwords required to pass unchanged. Every rule is traceable to the dictionary row and scan image that attest it.

An optional pass corrects common misuses of words, from the corrections marked in the 6-volume Uyghur edebiy tilining izahliq lughiti (1990-1999). Suffixes are re-derived against the replacement with vowel harmony, voicing assimilation and raising, and the tool declines rather than guesses where the derivation is not safe. Includes the map data, arbitrated word by word against the 2009 Hazirqi zaman Uyghur edebiy tilining imla lughiti dictionary of the Milletler Til-Yeziq Komiteti and 2011 Hazirqi zaman Uyghur tilining izahliq lughiti (qisqartilmisi), and checked against every headword of both, with hand-verified headwords required to pass unchanged. Every rule is traceable to the dictionary row and scan image that attest it.

title: Aether-Lang: a Rust runtime for topological machine learning
abstract: Aether-Lang is a Rust workspace for a small language runtime, a bounded topological computation core, ML primitives, and a sparse-event kernel prototype. The project uses topology as a systems signal: embeddings, residuals, binary streams, and scheduler state are converted into geometric or topological objects, then used for execution, diagnostics, convergence checks, or pruning. Includes a Lean 4 verified kernel.

title: 久那斗 Kunato Core Ver.3.0.0: Truth-Preserving Deliberation, Refutation Persistence, and Epistemic Boundary Control
abstract: Abstract We present Kunato Core Ver.3.0.0, a formal framework for truth-preserving deliberation, refutation persistence, grounded justification, dependency-safe rollback, and epistemic boundary control. Kunato v3 addresses a general problem in scientific reasoning, artificial intelligence, hypothesis management, and multi-agent deliberation: how a reasoning system can preserve constraints already established by semantics, evidence, refutation, and dependency analysis while remaining open to new claims and legitimate revision. The framework treats accepted knowledge as a protected epistemic state and separates proposition generation from authority to modify that state. Its governing rule is: no valid warrant, no epistemic state transition. Kunato distinguishes linguistic expressibility from model-theoretic constructibility. Given background-compatible worlds B and a candidate model set M(h), a hypothesis h is constructible only when B intersect M(h) is nonempty. Linguistic expression therefore does not by itself establish possibility. Semantic terms are versioned so that changes in definition constitute explicit semantic revisions rather than silent reinterpretations of previously evaluated claims. Under monotone evidence accumulation, the surviving model set S_t(h) is nonincreasing: S_(t+1)(h) is a subset of S_t(h). Once S_t(h) becomes empty, additional monotone evidence cannot revive the refuted hypothesis. Reopening instead requires an explicit revision of evidence, background constraints, semantic representation, or test validity, and reassessment does not itself constitute renewed support. This establishes a formal distinction between evidence accumulation and belief revision while preserving previously earned refutations under unchanged conditions. Kunato v3 implements a zero-trust epistemic architecture. External humans, language models, software agents, documents, and other generators may submit claims but cannot self-certify admission-critical properties such as constructibility, refutation status, independent support, semantic compatibility, or conflict status. These properties are derived by the verifier from declared registries. Accepted-state transitions require context-bound write certificates; stale, forged, context-mismatched, or proposition-mismatched authorization fails closed. Source identity alone provides no epistemic privilege when semantic and evidential conditions are otherwise identical. Support is represented through explicit alternative support sets and evaluated using grounded least-fixed-point semantics. Declared observations, discharged proof obligations, or trusted axiomatic roots initiate grounded support, whereas pure circular support cannot bootstrap epistemic authority. When premises are invalidated, a dependent claim remains justified if and only if at least one complete support set remains disjoint from the invalidated premises. Independently supported conclusions therefore survive rollback, while unsupported and false remain formally distinct categories. The framework establishes false-root closure and premise-laundering results. If every complete support path for a dependent closure ultimately contains the same invalid premise, invalidation of that premise eliminates all recorded justification within the closure. The worst-case rollback radius is unbounded as the dependency graph grows. Moreover, adding downstream mathematics, simulations, terminology, citations, intermediate propositions, computational complexity, or rhetorical elaboration cannot repair a support path that still contains an invalid premise. Only a genuinely independent support path can restore justified inferential authority. This yields a minimal stopping rule for reasoning branches whose indispensable roots have been invalidated. At the deliberative boundary, Kunato separates participation from epistemic write authority. Any unrestricted channel capable of bypassing verification makes the authorization invariant impossible to guarantee. Conversely, given sound declared roots, an intact verifier and certificate mechanism, complete mediation, and the specified transition function, the authorization invariant is preserved across every finite reachable transition sequence. A sequence of external inputs that never reaches ACCEPTED status has zero effect on the accepted-signature set. The framework therefore controls epistemic state transitions without requiring classification of participants by identity, intention, belief, religion, nationality, moral character, or presumed honesty. This architecture reaches an explicit fixed point rather than asserting absolute self-grounding. Any finite verification chain must ultimately terminate in trusted roots or become circular. Kunato therefore states its strongest guarantee conditionally: sound roots + intact verifier + complete mediation -> authorization invariant preserved. This fixed point also identifies the irreducible boundary of the framework. Internal authorization integrity does not imply ontological truth if trusted semantic or evidential roots are false, corrupted, or inadequate. Authenticated provenance is not equivalent to truth, and an arbitrarily mutable or bypassable verifier cannot guarantee accepted-core integrity. Kunato v3 therefore does not claim to be a truth oracle, a universal natural-language semantic compiler, or a detector of deceptive persons or intentions. Its formal objective is narrower: to prevent unsupported claims from acquiring epistemic authority within a protected reasoning state. The reference implementation computationally audits constructibility, evidence contraction, refutation persistence, self-attestation exclusion, source-identity independence, semantic drift, conflict quarantine, certificate integrity, grounded support, dependency-safe rollback, false-root propagation, premise-laundering resistance, fail-closed authorization, adversarial-stream noninterference, transition-invariant preservation, and the evidence-root boundary. The reported verification includes 34,782 dependency-safe rollback cases, 1,024 premise-laundering extensions, a 1,000-input non-accepted adversarial stream, and finite false-root dependency trees, with no recorded audit failures. Machine-readable results are reproducible byte-for-byte, including the terminal newline, across the tested Python hash seeds. Kunato Core Ver.3.0.0 thus defines an epistemic security kernel for scientific reasoning, AI-assisted research, automated hypothesis management, truth-maintenance systems, belief revision, knowledge-base integrity, and human-AI or multi-agent deliberation. Its fixed point is not absolute truth certification, but preservation of justified epistemic state relative to explicit semantic and evidential roots. The resulting operational principle is concise: preserve meaning, verify premises, retain valid refutations, reject self-certified authority, prune invalid roots, preserve independent support, and reason only over the grounded residual structure.

title: Exact Quantum Algebraic Preimage Inversion of $\text{Keccak-f}[25]$ via Parallel Cubic HOBO Decomposition and $\mathbb{F}_2$ Linear Reconstruction on a Superconducting Processor
abstract: We demonstrate the exact quantum algebraic inversion of a full 25-bit round of the $\text{Keccak-f}[25]$ permutation without classical heuristic optimization or ancilla-induced Hilbert space dilation. By exploiting the architectural structure of the sponge construction, the inversion of the nonlinear $\chi$-layer is mapped into five uncoupled 5-qubit Higher-Order Binary Optimization (HOBO) blocks executed concurrently across 25 physical qubits. Each block incorporates exact 3-body Pauli interactions ($Z_i Z_j Z_k$) synthesized via 4-CNOT unitary ladders, eliminating the energy bias and SWAP overhead inherent to quadratic Rosenberg reductions. Under a boundary-slowed Roland-Cerf adiabatic schedule optimized to $p=4$ Trotter layers ($T^*=4.5$) to prevent longitudinal $T_1$ relaxation, the quantum circuit was executed on the 156-qubit superconducting processor \texttt{ibm_marrakesh} (Job ID: \texttt{da1qaqsdedkc73ercj4g}). All five non-linear row preimages were simultaneously resolved within the top measured eigenspaces. Subsequent inversion of the linear diffusion layers ($\pi \circ \rho \circ \theta$) via Gauss-Jordan elimination over Galois Field $\mathbb{F}_2$ yielded the exact 25-bit secret preimage $A_{\text{secret}}$ ($F(A) \equiv Y$), validating deterministic algebraic recovery over a search space of $2^{25} \approx 3.35 \times 10^7$ configurations.

title: Explainable AI: ACombined XAI Framework for Interpreting Slice-Level Brain Tumour Classification Models
abstract: This study investigates how multiple Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques can be combined to improve the interpretability of a deep learning model for brain tumour analysis in magnetic resonance imaging. A custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed and trained on two-dimensional Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) slices derived from the BraTS 2021 dataset to perform slice-level binary classification, distinguishing slices that contain tumour tissue from slices that do not. It should be noted that non-tumour slices are not healthy controls, as they may originate from patients who have a brain tumour elsewhere in the volume. The improved model achieved a slice-level test accuracy of 91.24 percent; this figure reflects performance over individual 2D slices rather than patient-level or volume-level diagnosis. Three complementary XAI methods were applied: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Grad-CAM highlighted broad spatial regions of interest, LRP provided pixel-level relevance and SHAP quantified the contribution of individual features. Presented together, these methods offered layered, qualitatively complementary explanations ranging from coarse regions of interest to fine pixel-level detail, including cases where slices captured only partial views of a tumour. The combined presentation provided a more rounded view of the model’s behaviour than any single method considered in isolation, although the study does not yet provide a quantitative measure of explanation faithfulness. The work illustrates the potential of integrated XAI techniques to support transparency in AI-assisted medical image analysis, while acknowledging that clinical usefulness would require multi-sequence and three-dimensional analysis, quantitative evaluation of the explanations, and assessment by radiologists. These remain directions for future work.

title: Learning Integrative Domain-aware Knowledge for Prompt Tuning in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
abstract: Due to the significant distributional shifts between unseen test data and training data, pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP continue to struggle with adapting to downstream tasks. Existing approaches mainly align visual and textual embeddings to extract domain-invariant information. However, domain-invariant features inevitably contain source-private information, which hinders the model from capturing domain-relevant knowledge and causes inference to shift toward the source style. Moreover, strict distribution alignment of shared prompts overlooks sample-specific domain variations, resulting in insufficient learning on the target domain. To address these issues, we propose a novel method, called I ntegrative D omain-aware K nowledge P rompt T uning (IDKPT) . Our method consists of a domain-aware feature extraction module and an instance-level prompt alignment strategy. The former exploits domain representations to balance general knowledge with domain-invariant features, while injecting domain-specific information into suppressed channels of the visual encoder. The latter combines class-specific textual prompts with instance-level visual prompts, and applies contrastive learning within subdomains to construct a discriminative and well-separated feature space. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets (Office-Home, Office-31, VisDA-2017, Mini-DomainNet) demonstrate that IDKPT significantly enhances the domain adaptation performance of VLMs, validating its effectiveness. The code will be available at: https://github.com/Jhin237/IDKPT .

title: Understanding Curriculum Learning in Large Language Models via Cross-Difficulty Optimization Dynamics
abstract: Curriculum learning has been widely adopted in the post-training of large language models by organizing training data from easy to hard. However, its effectiveness varies substantially across reasoning tasks, suggesting that no single curriculum is universally optimal and raising a fundamental question: what determines when curriculum learning works? In this paper, we answer this question by analyzing the optimization dynamics induced by different curriculum schedules. We show that the transfer relationship between different difficulty levels characterizes the optimization dynamics induced by curriculum learning, which in turn explains the effectiveness of different curriculum schedules, and formalize this relationship as Relative Transfer, a principled measure of cross-difficulty knowledge transfer. Based on this measurement, we derive Transfer-aware Dynamic Curriculum Sampling (TDCS), which dynamically adjusts the sampling distribution according to the estimated transfer relationship throughout training. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that TDCS consistently outperforms representative scheduling strategies across different tasks, model scales, and training paradigms. More importantly, our work provides a unified optimization-based explanation of curriculum learning through cross-difficulty transfer.

title: Discretized Holonomy as an Encoding Primitive for Quantum Cryptography
abstract: Geometric phases in quantum systems give rise to holonomies associated with cyclic evolution. In mixed-state settings, these holonomies arise from Uhlmann parallel transport on the purification bundle of density operators and depend on the global geometry of density-operator trajectories. In this work we introduce discretized mixed-state holonomy as a geometric encoding primitive. The public object is a density-operator trajectory, while the encoded information resides in a finite family of purification gauges associated with the same holonomy conjugacy class. By discretizing the gauge freedom of the purification bundle, continuous mixed-state holonomy is converted into finite alphabets suitable for discrete key spaces. We formalize the resulting primitive through an operational observation model and establish several structural properties. First, the holonomy representative cannot in general be reconstructed from the density-operator trajectory alone. Second, under conjugation-invariant observation channels, different encoded symbols are indistinguishable at the level of base-space observables. Third, discretized holonomy alphabets admit stable decoding under bounded perturbations of the underlying trajectory. The construction is illustrated through explicit qubit realizations based on isospectral mixed-state loops, together with representative-level decoding mechanisms and finite holonomy alphabets. We further discuss symmetry breaking, frame leakage, and limitations arising in realistic implementations. These results isolate a primitive-level geometric encoding mechanism based on mixed-state quantum geometry and provide a structural foundation for future cryptographic constructions involving representative-level holonomy information.

title: Intermediate-Task Training for Cross-Lingual Code-Mixed Performance
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does intermediate-task training on code-related tasks (e.g., programming language understanding) affect zero-shot cross-lingual performance on XTREME-R for tasks involving code-mixed or code-switching text? title: mine:o1-nano Base Model Deployment: A 124M-Parameter Foundational Language Model Pre-Trained From Scratch on TPU Infrastructure
abstract: This paper presents the architectural design, pre-training methodology, and empirical evaluation of mine:o1-nano Base Model, a 124-million-parameter causal language model trained entirely from scratch by a solo founder at MineAI Technology. The project was undertaken as a first infrastructure proof point: to demonstrate that a small, resource-constrained team can independently execute a full pre-training run, including distributed TPU orchestration, checkpoint recovery, and durable off-platform storage, without relying on third-party model APIs. The model was trained using JAX and Flax (NNX) on a Google Cloud TPU v5e-8 pod slice accessed via Kaggle's free-tier notebook infrastructure, using explicit device-mesh sharding across 8 TPU cores. Training ran on the OpenWebText corpus (approximately 18.7 GB of raw text, corresponding to roughly 9.0 billion tokens) for the full 80,000-step schedule, reaching a final validation cross-entropy loss of approximately 3.09 and a perplexity of approximately 21.98. To the author's knowledge, and based on available public information, mine:o1-nano is among the first — if not the first — base language models trained fully from scratch by an individual in Pakistan. This report documents the engineering process, including real infrastructure failures encountered and resolved, as a transparent technical record.

The model was trained using JAX and Flax (NNX) on a Google Cloud TPU v5e-8 pod slice accessed via Kaggle's free-tier notebook infrastructure, using explicit device-mesh sharding across 8 TPU cores. Training ran on the OpenWebText corpus (approximately 18.7 GB of raw text, corresponding to roughly 9.0 billion tokens) for the full 80,000-step schedule, reaching a final validation cross-entropy loss of approximately 3.09 and a perplexity of approximately 21.98. To the author's knowledge, and based on available public information, mine:o1-nano is among the first — if not the first — base language models trained fully from scratch by an individual in Pakistan. This report documents the engineering process, including real infrastructure failures encountered and resolved, as a transparent technical record.

title: Dataset for Threat Intelligence in Dark Web Forums
abstract: Part I. Research and Purpose 1. Overview Dark web forums often surface discussion of vulnerabilities, targeted organizations, and emerging attack techniques before they appear in mainstream threat intelligence feeds. However, this text is high-volume, noisy, and dense with slang and platform-specific jargon, making manual analyst review difficult to scale. This dataset accompanies the study "Evaluating Open-Source Large Language Models for Emerging Threat Intelligence in Dark Web Forums." that is presented in International Conference on Cybernetics and Intelligent Systems (ICORIS) 2026. The study investigates whether open-source large language models, without task-specific fine-tuning, can reliably extract structured threat intelligence from raw forum discussion. 2. Research Objectives The study evaluates three open-source, 32-billion-parameter-class language models — Qwen3-32B, Gemma 4 31B-it, and GLM-4-32B-0414 — on their ability to extract four aspect types from forum threads: Vulnerabilities Organizations Countries Cyber threats Each model was prompted identically, using worked examples and a constrained output format. Extracted entities were normalized to a canonical form and, where an established reference exists, aligned to recognized standards: MITRE CWE → for vulnerability entities MITRE ATT&CK → for cyber threat/technique entities ISO 3166 country codes → for country entities Model outputs were benchmarked against a reference annotation set generated by GPT-5.4 nano, using Entity F1 and complementary metrics to assess extraction quality per aspect type. 3. Corpus and Methodology Summary Source platform: DarkForums Processing stages: Raw → Preprocessed (used for modeling) → Safe (PII-redacted, this release) Extraction approach: Zero/few-shot prompting with worked examples and constrained output schema, no model fine-tuning Reference/benchmark generation: GPT-5.4 nano used to produce gold-standard extraction reference Evaluation: Entity F1 and complementary metrics, computed per aspect type per model 4. Purpose of This Data Release This release publishes the Safe-tier forum corpus only, the underlying thread and post text, redacted of personal and credential/financial data per the scheme in Part II. It does not include the model extraction outputs, gold-standard annotations, or benchmark scores reported in the paper. Publishing the redacted corpus on its own supports: Independent extraction research → other researchers can apply their own information-extraction methods to authentic, privacy-safe dark web forum text. Comparative NLP research on model performance over noisy, adversarial, jargon-heavy text more broadly, beyond this paper's specific four aspect types. Methodological transparency → the redaction rules in Part II document exactly how personal data was removed, so other researchers can assess the corpus's safety and reuse the approach on similar sources. The entity annotations, per-model outputs, and Entity F1 benchmark results reported in the paper are not included in this release. Researchers who need them for exact reproduction of the paper's benchmark numbers, or who need the Preprocessed (pre-redaction) tier for pipeline validation, may contact the authors to discuss access under a data use agreement. 5. Important Notes on Dataset Content Offensive/hateful language: Some forum posts contain slurs or hateful language directed at individuals or groups. This language has been preserved verbatim (i.e., not redacted) to maintain research fidelity to the original forum discourse. Redaction in this dataset addresses personally identifiable and credential/financial information only (see Part II). Forum usernames retained: Poster handles (e.g., forum aliases of threat actors) are retained by default, as these pseudonymous personas are a research subject of the study rather than private individuals requiring protection. See Part II, Section 5.8 for the limited exceptions. No live malicious infrastructure: Working exploit code, active command-and-control addresses, and functional credential pairs are out of scope for this document but were independently reviewed prior to release; see Part II, Section 8 for related limitations. Redaction is not guaranteed perfect: The redaction process is rule- and pattern-based (Part II) with an automated residual-detection check built in, but breach-dump text is highly heterogeneous (multiple languages, multiple schema formats, inconsistent source formatting). A small number of residual instances may remain despite this process; see Part II, Section 8 for known limitations and the validation approach used before this release. 6. Dataset Composition This repository contains a single file: File Description safe_corpus.json DarkForums thread and post data (Safe tier), PII-redacted per the Part II scheme. One JSON object per line (JSON Lines format). 7. Dataset Feature Reference Forum Thread & Post Fields Field Type Description thread_id string Unique identifier for the forum thread on the source platform title string Thread title as posted category string Forum-assigned category (e.g., "Leaks") forum_name string Sub-forum/board name (e.g., "Databases") author string Handle of the thread-starting poster (pseudonymous forum persona, retained per Section 5) date_posted string Timestamp or relative time of thread creation, as captured at scrape time posts array List of reply posts within the thread (may be empty for title-only threads) posts[].post_id string Unique identifier for the individual post posts[].post_number string Sequential post number within the thread (e.g., "#1") posts[].author string Handle of the post's author posts[].post_date string Timestamp of the individual post posts[].content string Post body text, PII-redacted per Part II. Contains placeholder tokens (e.g., [PERSON], [EMAIL], [PHONE], [ADDRESS], [CREDENTIAL], [FINANCIAL]) in place of removed personal/credential data — see Part II, Section 4 for the full token taxonomy. 8. Standards Referenced MITRE CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration): https://cwe.mitre.org/ MITRE ATT&CK: https://attack.mitre.org/ ISO 3166 Country Codes: https://www.iso.org/iso-3166-country-codes.html 9. Full license text: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ This dataset was created for academic research purposes. While the CC-BY 4.0 license permits broader reuse, the authors request that it be used in a manner consistent with responsible academic research, given that the underlying text originates from real data-breach and cybercrime forum content. 11. Contact You can contact us directly at ventje.jeremias@binus.ac.id for data access requests (limited) under a data use agreement. Part II. PII Redaction Scheme Scope: Rules for transforming Preprocessed Data (modeling corpus, contains PII) into Safe Sample Data (this release). 1. Purpose The Preprocessed corpus (DarkForums "Leaks"/"Databases" threads) contains pasted excerpts of real data-breach dumps — SQL insert statements, CSV/delimited samples, and prose descriptions — that include real individuals' personal data. Before public release, this data was transformed so that no real person can be identified or contacted, and no credential or financial material is redistributed, while preserving everything needed to reproduce the paper's entity-extraction and benchmarking results. 2. Objectives Prevent re-identification of real individuals named or listed in breach dumps (victims' names, emails, phones, physical addresses, dates of birth, government IDs). Prevent redistribution of actionable credential/financial material → password hashes, salts, API keys/tokens, full card numbers, bank account numbers, even when technically "not PII," since these enable direct harm (account takeover, fraud) independent of identification risk. Preserve research utility. The four extraction aspects the study depends on → vulnerabilities, organizations, countries, cyber threats were not stripped. Company/website names, country names, malware/threat-actor-group names, and CVE/CWE/ATT&CK identifiers survive redaction untouched. Preserve threat-actor context. Forum usernames/handles (post authors) are pseudonymous personas central to threat intelligence, not private individuals' identities → they are generally retained, subject to the case-by-case check in Rule 5.8. Be deterministic and auditable. The same input always produces the same output; every redaction is traceable to a rule so a reviewer can audit false positives/negatives. Minimize over-redaction. Aggressive blanket redaction (e.g., stripping all capitalized words) would destroy the org/country/threat signal needed for modeling and defeat the paper's purpose, rules are targeted, not blunt. Handling of offensive/hateful language (e.g., slurs) is out of scope for this scheme. That content is kept verbatim in the Safe tier and disclosed in Part I, Section 5. 3. Data Profile (from sample analysis) Pattern Notes INSERT INTO ... VALUES SQL dumps Column list + positional tuples; contains real names, emails, password hashes Delimited "sample:" blocks (comma) e.g. breach CSV pasted inline, header row usually present Delimited "sample:" blocks (semicolon) e.g. card_id;full_nam

title: Knowledge-enhanced large language model construction for garlic cultivation using GraphRAG
abstract: Introduction: Rapid advances in smart agriculture have highlighted the potential of large language models (LLMs), while practical applications remain limited by privacy risks, high training costs, and hallucinations. Focusing on garlic cultivation, this study proposes a knowledge-graph-enhanced framework that improves domain-specific LLMs through graph-based retrieval. Methods: A hybrid clustering algorithm with intra-cluster multidimensional ranking is employed to identify ten core entity types from garlic-related corpora. Few-shot learning and chain-of-thought prompting are further integrated to optimize entity and relation extraction using Qwen 2.5:32B, leading to the construction of a structured garlic cultivation knowledge graph. The knowledge graph is integrated with LLMs via GraphRAG, while prompt reconstruction strategies are adopted to enrich contextual information and constrain generation, thereby improving domain grounding and reducing hallucinations. Results: Experimental results demonstrate absolute improvements of 13.0, 37.0, and 28.2 percentage points in precision, recall, and F1-score, respectively, for triple extraction compared with the baseline LLM, along with a 37.5 percentage point increase in retrieval-based question-answering accuracy. Discussion: The proposed approach is interpretable and locally deployable without dependence on commercial APIs, offering a transferable methodological reference for domain-specific knowledge graph construction and intelligent question answering across diverse crop systems.

title: A deep learning based speech assessment and pronunciation correction system for vocational English
abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, deep learning has been widely applied in education and shown great potential in language learning evaluation and personalized feedback. Aiming at the problems of single oral evaluation methods and lagging correction mechanism in higher vocational English teaching, this paper proposes a deep learning-based speech assessment and pronunciation correction system for vocational English. Focusing on speech signal processing, acoustic feature extraction, pronunciation deviation detection and correction feedback, the system integrates speech recognition, multi-dimensional acoustic feature modeling, forced speech alignment and fine-grained error positioning technologies. It realizes phoneme-level pronunciation error identification, frame-level speech difference comparison and multi-modal personalized correction feedback. This paper constructs the system architecture, optimizes the pronunciation error recognition algorithm based on CNN-BiLSTM, designs the dual-channel speech alignment mechanism combining DTW and Transformer, and establishes a multi-dimensional feedback generation strategy covering error description, standard pronunciation demonstration and targeted training guidance. Experimental results show that the system achieves 92.7% pronunciation error detection accuracy, with frame alignment deviation within ±0.08s and feedback delay less than 1.8s, and more than 85% of students recognize the effectiveness of correction feedback. The system can significantly improve the efficiency of oral English evaluation and the effect of pronunciation correction, providing an intelligent solution for real-time, personalized oral evaluation and targeted correction in higher vocational English teaching.

title: VERaiPHY -- Validation & Evaluation for Robust AI in PHYsics
abstract: Modern machine learning is leading to substantial gains in precision, flexibility, and computational efficiency in fundamental physics. Statistical validation, uncertainty quantification, and robustness assessment are less systematically addressed. The VERaiPHY initiative (Validation & Evaluation for Robust AI in PHYsics) is a series of articles developed within the PHYSTAT programme, aimed at establishing statistical standards for the development, evaluation, and deployment of ML techniques. Each article focuses on a specific methodological domain from a statistics perspective and clarifies statistical questions, tests, and the interpretation of results. This opening article establishes the probabilistic, statistical, and machine learning foundations that the later contributions assume, together with the notation used throughout.

title: Robustness of mT5-large in Code Generation Under Adversarial Attacks with Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer
abstract: Pre-trained multilingual language encoders, such as multilingual BERT and XLM-R, show great potential for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. However, these multilingual encoders do not precisely align words and phrases across languages. Especially, learning alignments in the multilingual embedding space usually requires sentence-level or word-level parallel corpora, which are expensive to be obtained for low-resource languages. An alternative is to make the multilingual encoders more robust; when fine-tuning the encoder using downstream task, we train the encoder to tolerate noise in the contex Research goal: How does the robustness of mT5-large to adversarial examples in code generation tasks differ between zero-shot cross-lingual transfer with and without intermediate-task training on XGLUE benchmarks, as measured by BLEU score drop under targeted attacks?
